vignette:
Patient: Mr. A.
Age: 77
Occupation: Retired School Principal
Marital Status: Married, 52 years
Trauma: Assault during a home invasion

Mr. A. is a tall, distinguished man who carries himself with a quiet dignity that seems to require a conscious effort. He sits very still, his hands resting on his knees, and his eyes scan the room in a slow, deliberate arc before he begins to speak. He retired three years ago after forty-two years as a principal, a man who built order out of chaos, who knew the name of every student and the rhythm of every school day. That job, he says, was about control and care. Now, he feels he has neither.

The story he tells begins on a Tuesday night, two years ago. He and his wife, Esther, had just finished watching the evening news. He was locking the back door, a ritual he had performed thousands of times. He heard a sound from the living room-a thump, a muffled cry from Esther. He turned, and a young man was there, holding a crowbar. He remembers the smell of sweat and cheap beer. He remembers the man's eyes, wide and frantic, not evil, just desperate. He remembers trying to step between the intruder and his wife. He does not remember the blow to his head, only the strange, silent white light that followed, and the sensation of the carpet against his cheek.

The physical wounds healed. The concussion cleared. But the world Mr. A. returned to is a different place. He no longer sleeps in the bedroom. He sleeps on the couch in the living room, facing the front door, with a heavy flashlight on the end table. "I need to see who is coming in," he explains, his voice level. "I need to see them first." He wakes every night at 2:47 AM, the time he believes the assault occurred. He lies perfectly still, listening to the creaks of the house, parsing each sound: the furnace kicking on is a footstep, the settling of the roof is a window being pried open. His heart hammers so hard he can feel it in his throat, a frantic, trapped bird. He does not wake Esther. He feels a fierce, protective shame about his fear. He was supposed to be the protector. He failed.

His days are structured by avoidance. He has not been to the grocery store since the assault. He cannot bear the crowds, the people moving too close, the sudden movements. His daughter drives Esther to run errands. He has stopped attending the mosque, a place that was the bedrock of his life. "The imam is a good man," he says, "but I cannot sit still. I am watching the door. I am watching the hands of the man next to me. I am not praying. I am waiting." His primary occupation now is vigilance. He walks a perimeter of his house three times a day, checking every lock, every window. He has installed a security system with five cameras, and he spends hours reviewing the footage, looking for anomalies, for threats that did not materialize.

He is irritable, a fact that pains him deeply. He was known for his patience, for his ability to de-escalate a fight between teenagers with a quiet word. Now, a sudden noise-a dropped pan in the kitchen-makes him snap. He shouts at Esther for startling him, then retreats to the garage, trembling with remorse. He feels a profound detachment. He looks at his grandchildren's photos and feels a numb affection, a memory of love rather than the feeling itself. The world has a film over it, a flatness. He describes it as "living behind a window."

When he talks about the future, he stops. He has no plans. He cannot imagine a vacation, a dinner out, a simple walk. The only future he can conceptualize is the next check of the locks, the next long, sleepless night. He holds his wife's hand when he speaks, a desperate, clinging grip. He is a man who built his life on order and community, now marooned on a small, terrified island of his own making, listening for a sound that has already come and gone.
